title: How animals choose partners: displays, songs, dances and nests

summary.text: A peacock's long tail makes flying harder, so why does he have it? In this unit you will watch pigeons at the window, test whether one change to a display changes what is chosen, test how a long tail slows flight, and play a call-and-answer game.
summary.art: A peacock with his train spread wide and shaking, and a brown peahen standing a little way off, looking past him at a second peacock.

intro.hook: A peacock's train is about one and a half metres long. A tiger can see the train from far away, and the train is heavy to carry. He sheds the train every year and grows a new one. Why does he grow something so costly?
intro.text: The peacock grows his train because peahens choose. A peahen walks past several peacocks, watches them, and picks one to be the father of her chicks. The things animals do to find and win a partner are called courtship. A magpie robin sings. Two sarus cranes dance. A weaver bird builds a nest and waits for a female to inspect it. In this unit you run a choosing test with paper trains. You also find out what a long tail costs a flyer.
intro.art: A row of three peacocks in a dry forest clearing, each with his train raised, and one peahen walking slowly past them.

outcomes: I can say what courtship is, and why animals need it.
I can explain how a call, a song or a flash helps an animal find their own species.
I can describe four kinds of courtship, with an animal for each: displays, songs, dances, and nests or gifts.
I can explain who chooses, and what a chooser can learn by watching a display.
I can test whether one change to a display changes what choosers pick, and say how sure I am.
I can explain what a display costs, using my Long Tail Test.
I can describe several ways that animals pair and raise young, and name an animal for each.
I can explain how scientists found out that animals choose, and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: Everything an animal does to find and win a partner for having young.
terms.example: A male pigeon puffs up his neck, bows and coos in front of a female. That is courtship.
terms.art: A male pigeon with a puffed-up neck bowing low in front of a second pigeon on a balcony wall.

terms.meaning: An animal's partner for having young. To mate means to join with a partner so that young can begin.
terms.example: A peahen chooses one peacock as her mate. Later she lays eggs.
terms.art: A peahen standing beside a peacock whose train is folded.

terms.meaning: One kind of living being. Animals of the same species can have young together.
terms.example: A house crow and a jungle crow look alike, but they are two species.
terms.art: A grey-necked house crow and an all-black jungle crow side by side on a wall.

terms.meaning: A show of colour, shape or movement that one animal gives for another to see.
terms.example: A peacock raising and shaking his train is giving a display.
terms.art: A peacock from the front with his train raised in a full fan.

terms.meaning: The very long feathers that grow from a peacock's back and cover his tail. They are not his tail feathers.
terms.example: A peacock's train has about 150 eyespots. His real tail is short and brown, and it holds the train up.
terms.art: A peacock seen from behind with his train raised, showing the short brown tail feathers that prop it up.

terms.meaning: A body part that is used for showing, more than for eating, moving or keeping warm.
terms.example: A peacock's train, a rooster's comb and a male bullfrog's blue throat sacs are ornaments.
terms.art: Three small pictures in a row: a peacock's eyespot feather, a rooster's red comb and a yellow bullfrog with blue throat sacs.

terms.meaning: A long or repeated pattern of sounds that an animal gives, most often in the breeding season.
terms.example: A male magpie robin sings from the top of a pole at sunrise.
terms.art: A black and white magpie robin singing on top of an electric pole at sunrise.

terms.meaning: A song or call that two partners give together, each one fitting their part to the other's.
terms.example: A pair of sarus cranes point their beaks at the sky and call together.
terms.art: Two tall grey sarus cranes with red heads standing side by side, beaks pointed up, calling.

terms.meaning: Food or another useful thing that one animal gives to a partner during courtship.
terms.example: A male kingfisher brings a fish and offers this gift to a female, head first.
terms.art: A small blue kingfisher holding a fish out to a second kingfisher on a branch over water.

terms.meaning: The part of the year when a species courts, mates and raises young.
terms.example: For many Indian frogs, the breeding season starts with the first heavy monsoon rain.
terms.art: Yellow bullfrogs gathered in a rain pool under dark monsoon clouds.

terms.meaning: A place where many males gather and display close together, and females come to choose among them.
terms.example: Blackbuck males gather on a lek in the grassland of Velavadar in Gujarat.
terms.art: Several male blackbuck with spiral horns standing a few steps apart on open grassland, with females walking between them.

terms.meaning: The lasting tie between two animals who stay together to raise young.
terms.example: A pair of great hornbills may stay together for many years.
terms.art: Two great hornbills with large yellow beaks sitting close together on a fig branch.

explanations.concept: Courtship: finding and winning a partner
explanations.definition: Courtship is everything an animal does to find and win a partner for having young.
explanations.description: Most animals have two parents. A new animal begins when two tiny cells join. One cell, the egg, comes from the mother. The other comes from the father. So before any young can begin, two animals must find each other and accept each other. Courtship does three jobs. It helps an animal find a partner of their own species. It shows that the animal is ready to breed now. It gives the other animal time to judge and to choose. Courtship can be a display of colour, a song, a dance, a nest or a gift. Many animals use several of these together. Humans are animals too. People also sing, dress up, dance and give gifts to someone they hope to marry.
examples: A male pigeon bows and coos in front of a female on a balcony.
A male magpie robin sings from a rooftop every morning in the breeding season.
A pair of sarus cranes bow and leap together in a wet field.
explanations.art: A balcony wall with one pigeon bowing and turning, and another pigeon watching with her head tilted.

explanations.definition: Each species has their own courtship code: a pattern of calls, flashes, colours or moves that others of that species know.
explanations.description: A pond in the monsoon may hold five species of frogs, all calling at once. A female must find a male of her own species, because only then can her eggs grow into young. So each species of frog has a different call. One gives slow, deep calls. Another gives fast clicks. The female goes towards the pattern of her own species and passes the others by. Crickets do the same with their chirps, and fireflies do the same with flashes of light. Each firefly species flashes in a rhythm of their own. A code like this saves time and energy for both partners. It is also the first question in every courtship: are you my kind?
examples: Indian bullfrogs and small cricket frogs call in the same pond, with different calls.
Two species of firefly in one field flash in different rhythms.
A female cricket walks towards the chirp pattern of her own species.
explanations.art: A pond at night with two kinds of frog calling, and a female frog swimming towards the one of her own kind.

explanations.definition: A display is a show of colour, shape or movement that one animal gives for another to see.
explanations.description: A peacock lifts his train into a fan and turns to face a peahen. Then he shakes the train about 25 times each second, so that it rustles and the eyespots seem to shimmer. A male Indian bullfrog turns bright yellow after the first heavy monsoon rain. His two throat sacs turn deep blue. The colour lasts only a day or two. A male fan-throated lizard in Maharashtra flicks out a blue, black and orange throat fan. Many of these colours are shown only in the breeding season, or only for a moment. A peacock's blue and green are a special case. His feathers hold only a brown colouring. The tiniest parts of each feather are stacked in neat rows, far too small to see. These rows reflect blue and green light. This is called structural colour.
examples: A peacock raises his train and shakes it so that it rustles.
A male Indian bullfrog turns yellow after the first heavy rain.
A fan-throated lizard flicks out a bright throat fan on a stone.
explanations.art: A bright yellow male bullfrog with two blue throat sacs sitting in shallow rainwater beside a dull green female.

explanations.definition: A song is a long or repeated pattern of sounds. In courtship, a song tells others who is singing, where they are and that they are ready to breed.
explanations.description: Sound travels round leaves and walls, and it works in the dark. So a song can reach a partner who cannot see the singer. A male magpie robin sings from a high perch at sunrise. His song tells females that he is there. It also tells other males that this place is taken. The male koel calls 'ku-oo, ku-oo' through the hot months. Male frogs and crickets call at night. Singing takes energy, and a bird who sings for an hour is not feeding for that hour. People once thought that only male birds sing. In 2014 a team led by Karan Odom checked songbirds across the world. They found that females sing in about seven out of ten of the species with good records. In some species the two partners sing a duet.
examples: A male magpie robin sings from the top of a coconut tree at dawn.
A male koel calls 'ku-oo' from a mango tree in April.
A pair of sarus cranes call together in a duet.
explanations.art: A magpie robin singing on a rooftop water tank at dawn, with a second magpie robin listening from a nearby wire.

explanations.definition: A courtship dance is a set of moves that an animal makes for a partner. Two partners may also dance together.
explanations.description: The sarus crane is the tallest flying bird in the world, about as tall as a grown woman. A pair of sarus cranes bow to each other, spread their wings and leap into the air. They toss grass and sticks. They also call together in a duet. Sarus pairs stay together for many years, and they go on dancing long after they first pair up. So a dance is not only for winning a partner. It also keeps a pair bond strong. Great crested grebes, who are water birds, face each other and shake their heads in turn. Each partner copies the other. Julian Huxley described this dance in 1914. He saw that the male and the female both display, and both choose.
examples: Two sarus cranes bow and leap together in a paddy field in Uttar Pradesh.
Flamingos in the Rann of Kutch march side by side in a big group, turning their heads together.
A pair of great crested grebes shake their heads at each other on a lake.
explanations.art: Two sarus cranes in a flooded field, one leaping with wings spread and the other bowing low.

explanations.definition: Some animals court with something they have made or found: a nest, a decorated place or a gift of food.
explanations.description: A male baya weaver bird weaves a hanging nest from strips of grass or paddy leaf. When the nest is half built, he hangs under it, flaps his wings and calls. A female comes and inspects the nest and the place where it hangs. If she accepts, he finishes the nest and she lays her eggs inside. A male satin bowerbird in Australia builds two walls of sticks on the ground, called a bower. The bower is not a nest. He decorates the ground around it with blue things, such as feathers, flowers and bottle caps. A male white-spotted pufferfish, about 12 centimetres long, shapes a circle of ridges in the sand of the sea floor. The circle is about 2 metres wide and takes him about a week. A male kingfisher brings a fish to a female. A gift of food shows that the giver can find food.
examples: A male baya weaver hangs under his half-built nest and flaps his wings.
A satin bowerbird lays blue bottle caps in front of his bower.
A male kingfisher offers a small fish to a female.
explanations.art: A male baya weaver with a yellow head hanging under a half-built grass nest, with a brown female perched on the rim looking in.

explanations.concept: Who chooses, and what the chooser learns
explanations.definition: In courtship, at least one partner chooses. A chooser watches or listens, compares, and accepts or refuses.
explanations.description: In many species the female chooses. A peahen visits several peacocks before she accepts one. She will put a great deal into her eggs and chicks, so a poor choice costs her a lot. A display can tell a chooser several things. It shows that the other animal is of her species. A bright, full display is hard to grow or to keep up when an animal is ill or hungry. So it may also show good health. A well-made nest shows skill, and a gift shows that the giver can find food. In other species both partners choose, as sarus cranes and grebes do. In a few species the usual roles are swapped. A female greater painted-snipe is brighter than the male, and she courts him. He then sits on the eggs and looks after the chicks.
examples: A peahen walks away from two peacocks and stays near a third.
A female baya weaver inspects several half-built nests before she accepts one.
A bright female painted-snipe displays to a duller male.
explanations.art: A peahen walking along a line of three displaying peacocks, with small footprints showing that she has already passed two of them.

explanations.definition: A cost is anything an animal gives up or risks. Displays cost energy, time and safety.
explanations.description: Growing a long train or a long tail takes food. Singing for hours takes energy, and the singer is not feeding in that time. A bright colour or a loud call can also be noticed by a hunter. Male tungara frogs in Central America add a 'chuck' sound to their call. Females prefer calls with chucks. Bats who eat frogs also find those calls more easily. So every display is a balance between being chosen and staying alive. Many animals lower the cost. A peacock folds his train when he is not displaying, and he sheds it after the breeding season. A fan-throated lizard keeps his throat fan folded away. A male baya weaver has a yellow head only in the breeding season.
examples: A male long-tailed widowbird in Kenya flies slowly, with a tail half a metre long.
A calling frog is easier for a bat to find.
A peacock sheds his whole train after the breeding season.
explanations.art: A calling frog in a pool at night with a bat swooping down towards the sound.

explanations.definition: The breeding season is the part of the year when a species courts, mates and raises young.
explanations.description: Young animals need a lot of food. So most animals court at a time that puts their young into the world when food is plentiful. Earth is tilted, and this gives us seasons with longer and shorter days. Many birds can sense the length of the day. When the days grow longer, their bodies make chemical messengers called hormones. The hormones start the singing and the nest building. In much of India the monsoon sets the time. Peacocks display most as the rains come. Frogs call after the first heavy rain, because their tadpoles need pools. Baya weavers build when the paddy and the grass are long and green. So the timing of a peacock's dance depends on the monsoon rains, and on the tilt of the Earth that gives us the seasons.
examples: Peacocks call and display most at the start of the monsoon.
Bullfrogs gather to call after the first heavy rain.
Baya weavers start to weave when the grass grows long.
explanations.art: A peacock displaying on a low wall under dark rain clouds, with the first raindrops falling.

explanations.concept: Many ways to pair and raise young
explanations.definition: Species differ in how many partners an animal has, how long partners stay together, and who looks after the young.
explanations.description: There is no single way that animals live together. Sarus cranes and great hornbills live as pairs for many years. A hornbill mother seals herself inside a tree hollow with her eggs. The father brings fruit to her and the chick for about four months. A peacock does no nest work at all. He displays, several peahens choose him, and each peahen raises her chicks alone. A female bronze-winged jacana keeps a patch of lake and may have several male partners there. Each male sits on a set of her eggs and cares for the chicks. On the island of Oahu in Hawaii, about one third of the Laysan albatross pairs are two females. The two females raise a chick together, year after year. Each of these ways works for the species that lives that way.
examples: A pair of great hornbills raise one chick together.
A peahen raises her chicks without the peacock.
A male bronze-winged jacana leads the chicks across lotus leaves.
explanations.art: Four small scenes in one frame: a hornbill passing fruit into a slit in a tree, a peahen with chicks, a jacana father with chicks on lotus leaves, and two albatrosses sitting beside one chick.

explanations.concept: Why do choosers like what they like?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that animals choose partners, and that choosing over many generations has shaped trains, songs and dances. They disagree about why a chooser prefers one display to another.
explanations.description: A peahen prefers some peacocks to others. What is her preference about? There are three main answers, and working scientists hold each of them. More than one may be true at once.
examples: Peahens stay near some peacocks and walk away from others.
Female widowbirds nest most with the males who have the longest tails.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say a display is a report on health, such as Amotz Zahavi, William Hamilton and Marlene Zuk
perspectives.explanation: A big, bright display is costly. Only a healthy, well-fed animal can grow one and stay alive. So a chooser who picks the best display gets a healthy partner, and her young may be healthy too.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say beauty is enough, such as Charles Darwin, Ronald Fisher and Richard Prum
perspectives.explanation: Animals feel pleasure in certain colours, sounds and moves. If most females like long tails, then males with long tails are chosen more often. Their sons inherit the long tails, and their daughters inherit the liking for them. So a liking can spread and grow, even if the tail says nothing about health.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say the senses came first, such as Michael Ryan
perspectives.explanation: A chooser's eyes, ears and brain were already tuned to notice some things, such as the colour of ripe fruit. A display that matches what the senses already notice gets more attention.

explanations.art: A peahen with three thought bubbles above her: a healthy chick, a shimmering feather, and a bright berry.

agreed.text: Animals choose their partners, and in many species the female does most of the choosing.
agreed.evidence: In 1982 Malte Andersson made the tails of some male widowbirds longer and others shorter. Females nested most with the males whose tails he had made longer.

agreed.text: Each species has a courtship code of their own, which helps partners of the same species find each other.
agreed.evidence: Scientists play recorded calls from a speaker. Female frogs and crickets walk towards the call of their own species and ignore the others.

agreed.text: Choosing by partners, over many generations, has shaped ornaments such as long tails, bright colours and long songs.
agreed.evidence: Chosen animals have more young, and the young inherit their parents' features. Charles Darwin set this idea out in 1871, and many tests since then have supported it.

agreed.text: Displays have costs in energy, time and safety.
agreed.evidence: Bats who eat frogs find calling frogs more easily. Michael Ryan and Merlin Tuttle showed this with tungara frogs in Panama in the 1980s.

agreed.text: Females sing in many species of songbird.
agreed.evidence: A study led by Karan Odom in 2014 checked the songbird species with good records. Females sang in about seven out of ten of them.

agreed.text: Animals pair and raise young in many different ways, and no one way is the rule.
agreed.evidence: Field studies have followed marked animals for years. They show lasting pairs in cranes and hornbills. They show peahens raising chicks alone, and jacana fathers raising chicks alone.

challenging.claim: A peahen chooses the peacock with the most eyespots.
challenging.who: Marion Petrie and her team in England, in 1991 and 1994.
challenging.for: In their study, males with more eyespots won more mates. When they cut 20 eyespots from some trains, those males won fewer mates than the year before.
challenging.against: Mariko Takahashi's team watched peafowl in Japan for seven years and found no such preference. Peacocks differ very little in eyespot number, so peahens may judge something else, such as the shaking or the call.

challenging.claim: Only males display, and only females choose.
challenging.for: In peafowl and many other species, the male has the ornament and the female chooses.
challenging.against: Both partners display in cranes and grebes. Females sing in most songbird species. In painted-snipes and jacanas the female is the brighter one and she courts the male.

challenging.claim: A peacock's long train makes flying much harder for him.
challenging.who: A common belief, and some scientists.
challenging.for: The train is long and adds weight. Growing it each year takes food.
challenging.against: In 2014 Graham Askew filmed peacocks taking off with and without their trains. They rose just as fast with the train. The train still has other costs, such as the food needed to grow it.

challenging.claim: A costly display proves that an animal is healthy.
challenging.who: Amotz Zahavi, who called this the handicap principle in 1975.
challenging.for: Sick or hungry animals often have duller colours and shorter songs. Alan Grafen showed in 1990 that the idea can work in mathematics.
challenging.against: In 2020 Dustin Penn and Szabolcs Szamado argued that the idea is mistaken. They say that a signal can be honest without being wasteful.

challenging.claim: Birds who pair for life never change partners.
challenging.who: A common saying about swans, cranes and doves.
challenging.for: Many pairs of cranes, albatrosses and hornbills do stay together for many years.
challenging.against: Scientists who follow marked birds find that some pairs part, most often after a year when no chick was raised. A bird whose partner dies usually finds a new one.

challenging.claim: A female weaver bird chooses the male who weaves best.
challenging.who: A common belief about baya weavers.
challenging.for: Females inspect the half-built nests closely and pull at them.
challenging.against: Suhel Quader studied baya weavers in India and published the work in 2006. He found that the place mattered more than the weaving. Females preferred nests hung high, on thorny trees and on thin branches.

big_questions.q: Is a peacock's train beautiful by itself, or only when someone is looking at it?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides. A peahen, a tiger and a person each look at the same train.

big_questions.q: A peahen cannot tell us why she chose. How could we ever find out?
big_questions.hint: In the Eyespot Test you changed one thing and counted choices. What else could a scientist change?

big_questions.q: If a display puts an animal in danger, why has the display not disappeared?
big_questions.hint: An animal who lives long but is never chosen leaves no young.

big_questions.q: Sarus cranes go on dancing together for years. What might the dance do for them?
big_questions.hint: People who live together also keep doing small things for each other.

big_questions.q: Animals pair and raise young in many ways. Is any one way the natural one?
big_questions.hint: Compare hornbills, peafowl, jacanas and albatrosses. Each way works for that species.

big_questions.q: Humans are animals who also sing, dress up and give gifts. How much of that is courtship?
big_questions.hint: People also sing and dress up for friends, for festivals and for themselves.

story.title: The Half-Built Nest
story.note: Yazhini, her grandmother and the birds at their well are made up. These facts are real. Male baya weavers grow yellow heads in the breeding season. They weave hanging nests from strips of paddy leaf or grass, often over water. When a nest is half built, the male hangs under it, flaps his wings and calls. A female goes inside, pulls at it and looks around before she accepts or leaves. After she accepts, he adds the long entrance tube. What the female in the story is thinking is imagined.
text: Paati pulled once, and Yazhini's box came apart.

It had taken Yazhini three evenings. Her grandmother sold palm-leaf boxes at the Friday market in Tirunelveli, and this year Yazhini had asked to learn. She had split the dry palmyra leaf into strips. She had woven the strips over and under until her fingers were sore. Now the bottom of her first box hung open like a mouth.
"It looked fine," Yazhini said. Her voice shook.

"It looked fine," Paati agreed. "But somebody will carry murukku home in it for her children, on a bus, on a bad road. Looking fine is where a box starts." She put the strips back in Yazhini's lap and went in to stir the kuzhambu.
Yazhini did not want to look at the strips. She walked to the old well at the edge of the paddy field, where nobody would ask her about boxes.
A palmyra tree leaned over the well. From its lowest leaves hung six green shapes that had not been there last week.
They were nests, but they were not finished. Each one looked like a small helmet with a strap across the bottom. They were woven from thin strips of paddy leaf, still fresh and green.

On the nearest one sat a bird the size of a sparrow, with a head as yellow as turmeric. He held a strip in his beak that was longer than his whole body. He pushed it under one strand and pulled it over the next. Under, over. Under, over.
He is doing what I do, Yazhini thought. And he has no fingers.
Then a small flock dropped out of the sky and landed along the leaves. These birds were brown and streaked, with no yellow at all. They were the females.

The six yellow-headed males seemed to go mad. Each one swung under his own half-built nest, beat his wings as fast as he could, and called, a wheezy chee-ee-ee. All six called at once. Yazhini laughed out loud.
One brown female flew to the nearest nest. The male beat his wings even harder. She did not look at him. She went inside.

The nest shook. Yazhini could see the female's beak through the weave. She pulled at one strand, then at another. She pushed her head against the wall. She leaned out and looked down at the dark water far below. She looked up at the thin leaf-tip that held the whole nest. She did not hurry. The male had stopped calling. He only hung there and waited.
Then she flew to the next nest.
"Oh," said Yazhini. She felt it in her stomach. She knew exactly how three evenings of weaving felt.
The male sat on his nest for a while. Then he dropped down to the paddy, bit the edge of a leaf and flew up, tearing a long strip free. He went back to his weaving. Under, over.
The female was inside the third nest now. She pulled. She pushed. She looked down, and she looked up.

Yazhini watched her and stopped feeling sorry for the first male. Where would this bird's eggs lie? In that small woven room, over a deep well, through weeks of wind and rain. Then the chicks would lie there, getting heavier every day. If one strand gave way, there would be nothing under them but water.
She is not asking whether the nest looks fine, Yazhini thought. She is asking whether it will hold.

The female stayed in the third nest. She came to the opening and sat there. The male of that nest stopped beating his wings. He sang a long, soft song, quite different from the wheeze. Then he flew down for another strip. By tomorrow he would be weaving the long tube that makes the doorway.
Yazhini ran all the way home. Paati was on the thinnai with a heap of leaf beside her.
"Paati! The weaver birds at the well. The female goes inside and pulls at the nest before she takes it. She pulls just like you!"

Paati laughed until she had to put down her knife. "Who do you think I learned it from? My own paati sent me to that well when I was your age. Those birds were weaving before anybody's grandmother was born."
Yazhini sat down and picked up her strips. They were only a little bent.
"Under, over," she said. "Tighter this time. And when it is done, Paati, you must pull."
"I will pull," said Paati.
"Pull hard," said Yazhini.
story.epiphany: Yazhini was hurt when her grandmother pulled her box apart. Then she saw a female weaver bird pull at a nest and leave. The female was checking whether the nest would keep her eggs and chicks safe over the water. A chooser tests the things that will matter to her young.
ask: Why did the female weaver look down at the water and up at the leaf-tip?
The first male was refused. What did he do next, and why might that help him?
What is the same about choosing a nest and testing a box before market day?

games.title: Call and Answer: find your own kind
games.context: This is a listening game with knocks on a steel tumbler. Each animal has a call code, and you must tell which animal is calling. Real frogs, crickets and birds find partners of their own species in the same way.

setup.art: Six small cards in a row on a table, each with an animal's name on the front, and a steel tumbler with a spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the six call cards. Put a steel tumbler and a spoon on the table.

setup.art: A grown-up hiding one card behind her hand and knocking on the tumbler with the spoon, while a child listens with a code sheet in front of her.
setup.caption: 2. The caller knocks one card's code. The listener looks at the code sheet.

setup.art: The child knocking on her own tumbler in reply and pointing at one animal on the code sheet.
setup.caption: 3. The listener knocks the same code back and names the animal.

rules: One player is the caller. The others are listeners. Each listener has a code sheet. A 'wait' in a code is a slow count of two.
The caller shuffles the six cards and takes the top one in secret. The caller knocks that card's code on the tumbler with the spoon, twice.
A listener who knows the animal knocks the same code back and says the animal's name. A right answer scores 1 point.
Round 1 is quiet. Play all six cards.
Round 2 is the noisy pond. Play all six cards again with music or a mixer running, or with a second caller knocking another code.
Round 3 has strangers. The caller sometimes knocks a made-up code that is not on the sheet. The listener must say 'not my kind' to score.
After three rounds, the listener with the most points wins. With two players, swap roles and compare your scores.

flow.do: Cut out the six cards. Give the code sheet to your child. Knock each code once slowly, and let your child follow it on the sheet.
flow.say: Each animal on this sheet has a call code. I made the codes up, but real animals do have their own patterns. Listen to each one once.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Listen to each code once. Follow it on your sheet.
flow.parent: The codes are made up for the game. Real calls differ in the same way, by how many sounds come together and how long the gaps are.
flow.context: This is the first step of Call and Answer. You learn the six knock codes.

flow.do: Play round 1. Shuffle the cards, take one in secret and knock its code twice. Your child knocks it back and names the animal. Play all six cards.
flow.say: I am calling from across a pond. Which animal am I? Knock my code back to me, and then say my name.
flow.kid: Listen to the knocks. Knock the same code back. Say the animal's name.

ask.q: How did you tell the cricket's code from the koel's code?
good: I counted the knocks in each group.
The cricket has two groups of three.
I listened for the waits.

flow.context: In this step of Call and Answer you play round 1 in a quiet room.

flow.do: Play round 2 with music or a mixer running. Play all six cards again. Compare the score with round 1.
flow.say: Now the pond is noisy. Many animals are calling at once. Can you still pick out my code?
flow.kid: Now there is noise. Listen hard. Knock the code back.
flow.parent: Most listeners score lower in noise. Ask what would help. Louder knocks, a longer call and more repeats are all things real frogs do.
flow.context: In this step of Call and Answer you play round 2 with noise in the room.

flow.do: Play round 3. For two of the six turns, knock a code that is not on the sheet, such as 2, 4. Your child should say 'not my kind'. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: This time a stranger may call. If the code is not on your sheet, say 'not my kind' and do not answer.
flow.kid: Some codes are strangers. If a code is not on your sheet, say 'not my kind'.

check.q: Why does each species of frog have a call of their own?
options: So partners of one species find each other
So every frog can be the loudest
check.why: A female's eggs can grow into young only with a male of her own species. A call that differs from every other species leads her to the right partner. Loudness helps a call to carry, but the pattern is what tells her who is calling.

flow.context: This is the last step of Call and Answer. You play round 3, where some calls come from strangers.

items: Player ___ : turn 1 ___, turn 2 ___, turn 3 ___, turn 4 ___, turn 5 ___, turn 6 ___, turn 7 ___, turn 8 ___. Total ___
