rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and put them in a pile, face down. Players take turns.
On your turn, turn over the top card. If it is a display card, lay it in front of you. Its points are now at risk.
You may turn over another card, and another. Add the points of all the display cards in front of you.
You may stop at any time. Then you write this turn's points on the score page, and they are safe.
If you turn over a HAWK card, you lose all the points of this turn. Points from earlier turns stay safe.
After each turn, put the used cards back into the pile and shuffle the whole pile again.
The first player to reach 20 safe points is chosen and wins. Playing alone? Take 8 turns, write down your total, and then try to beat it.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them. Read the rules together. Play one practice turn each with the cards face up.
flow.say: Each display card earns points towards being chosen. A bigger display earns more. But a hawk card takes away the points of that turn.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Play one practice turn.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hawk Overhead. You set up the cards and learn the rules.

flow.do: Play until someone reaches 20 safe points, or for 8 turns each. Write the points kept after every turn.
flow.say: It is your turn. Turn over a card. Will you stop and keep your points, or will you risk one more card?
flow.kid: Turn over cards. Stop when you want. Write down the points you keep.

ask.q: How do you decide when to stop?
good: I stop when I have a lot to lose.
I stop after three cards.
There are 6 hawks in 24 cards, so each card is a risk.

flow.parent: Do not teach a best plan. Let your child try a bold plan and a careful plan, and compare the totals.
flow.context: In this step of Hawk Overhead you play the game and write down the points you keep.

flow.do: Look at the score page together. Ask which turns lost points. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the turns where you lost your points. How many cards had you turned over by then? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Which turns lost points? How many cards had you turned over?

check.q: In Hawk Overhead, what does a hawk card stand for?
options: A hunter who notices a display
check.why: A display is easy for a partner to notice, and also easy for a hunter to notice. The more an animal displays, the greater that risk. If you chose 'a partner who refuses', remember that a refusal costs time but not safety.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hawk Overhead. You look at your scores and think about risk.

experiments.title: The Eyespot Test: does one change alter what choosers pick?
experiments.question: Three paper trains are the same in every way except the number of spots: 4, 8 or 16. Do choosers pick one of them more often than the others? Or do they pick by where a train lies on the table?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which paper train will most choosers pick: the one with 4 spots, with 8 spots or with 16 spots? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three sheets of the same paper. Use dots of one size and one colour, and spread them evenly on each sheet. Only the number of dots differs. Bring the choosers in one at a time, so that nobody copies anyone else. Ask every chooser the same question in the same words. Give each one a slow count of five to look. Change the left-to-right order of the trains for every chooser. Do not tell the choosers what differs until the end.
results_table: Order of the trains from left to right
Place chosen: left, middle or right

materials.item: sheets of the same plain paper, such as A4 sheets or pages from one notebook
round sticker bindis of one size and one colour. You can also draw the dots with one felt pen, round a small coin
a table or a clear patch of floor
a pencil and a notebook page for the results
choosers: people at home, neighbours, or relatives who look at a photo on a phone. Six is the least, and ten or more is better

experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each chooser. Write the order of the trains, the train chosen and the place chosen. At the end, count the picks for each train and for each place.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three paper trains that differ only in the number of spots. Then you ask at least six people to choose one, and you count the choices. Marion Petrie tested peahens in a similar way.

setup.art: Three sheets of white paper side by side on a table, the first with 4 red dots, the second with 8 and the third with 16, all evenly spread.
setup.caption: 1. Stick 4 dots on one sheet, 8 on the next and 16 on the last.

setup.art: A woman walking into a room towards a table where three dotted sheets lie in a row, while a child stands behind the table with a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Bring in one chooser at a time. Ask: 'Which train would you pick?'

setup.art: A child's hands swapping the places of the three dotted sheets on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Change the order of the trains before the next chooser comes.

setup.art: A notebook page with a tally: three rows labelled 4 spots, 8 spots and 16 spots, with pencil strokes beside each.
setup.caption: 4. Count the picks for each train, and for each place on the table.

flow.do: Tell your child the plan. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will make three paper trains with 4, 8 and 16 spots. Then we will ask people to choose one. Which train will most people pick? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three paper trains have 4, 8 and 16 spots. Which will most people pick? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think choosers will pick that train?
good: More spots look richer.
Too many spots look messy.
People may not care about spots at all.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Nobody knows what your choosers will do, and that is why it is worth testing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eyespot Test. You guess which paper train most choosers will pick.

flow.do: Lay the three sheets the same way round. Stick 4 dots on the first, 8 on the second and 16 on the third. Spread the dots evenly over each sheet. Write a small 4, 8 or 16 on the back.
flow.say: These are our three trains. They must be the same in every way except one. What is the one thing that differs?
flow.kid: Stick 4 dots on one sheet. Stick 8 on the next. Stick 16 on the last.
flow.parent: If you draw the dots, use one pen and draw round the same coin each time. A dot of another size or colour would be a second change.
flow.context: In this step of the Eyespot Test you make three paper trains that differ only in the number of spots.

flow.do: Lay the trains in a row. Bring in one chooser. Say the question below, and count slowly to five. Record the order, the train chosen and the place. Change the order. Repeat with at least six choosers.
flow.say: Please look at these three paper trains for a count of five. Which one would you pick as the finest? Just point to it.
flow.kid: Bring in one chooser. Ask which train they pick. Write it down. Change the order.

check.q: Why do you change the order of the trains for each chooser in the Eyespot Test?
options: So the place does not sway the result
So the choosers have more fun
check.why: Some people tend to pick the middle thing, or the one nearest their hand. If the 16-spot train always lay in the middle, you could not tell which reason won. Changing the order separates the two. If you chose 'more fun', remember that a fair test changes only one thing on purpose.

flow.parent: For relatives on the phone, take three photos with the trains in three different orders. Send a different photo to each person. Ask them to reply with left, middle or right.
flow.context: In this step of the Eyespot Test you ask each chooser to pick one train, and you record the choice.

flow.do: Count the picks for each train. Then count the picks for each place: left, middle and right. Write both counts down.
flow.say: Count how many choosers picked each train. Now count how many picked the left, the middle and the right. Which count is more uneven?
flow.kid: Count the picks for each train. Then count the picks for each place.
flow.parent: With 6 choosers, luck alone would give about 2 picks to each train. A count of 4 or more for one train is worth noticing. A count of 3 is not.
flow.context: In this step of the Eyespot Test you count the choices by train and by place.

flow.do: Ask your child for the three things below. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did the number of spots change the choices? How sure are you, with this many choosers?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: How could you become more sure of your result?
good: Ask more choosers.
Run the test again on another day.
Check that the place on the table did not decide.

ask.q: You tested people. What would you need to do to test peahens?
good: Change real trains and watch what peahens do.
Count which peacocks the peahens stay with.

flow.parent: There is no right result here. In many homes the 16-spot train gets the most picks, and in some the 8-spot train does. Write down what you found. The explanation: you changed one thing and counted choices. Scientists must work in the same way, because a peahen cannot say what she prefers. In 1994 Marion Petrie and Tim Halliday cut 20 eyespots from the trains of some peacocks. Those males won fewer mates than they had the year before. A later study in Japan did not find that peahens prefer more eyespots, so the question is still open.
flow.think: If you took 8 dots off the 16-spot train, would the same choosers still pick it?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Eyespot Test. You say what your counts show about spots and choosers.

experiments.title: The Long Tail Test: does a long tail make flying harder?
experiments.question: A paper bird is thrown with no tail, with a 30 centimetre tail and with a 60 centimetre tail. Does the length of the tail change how far the paper bird flies?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will fly farthest: the paper bird with no tail, with the short tail or with the long tail? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one paper bird for the whole test, so that the folds are the same. The same person throws every time, from the same line, with the same gentle push. Throw five times for each tail, because one throw can be a fluke. Use strips of the same newspaper and the same width. Only the length of the tail changes. At the end, throw three more times with no tail. This checks that the paper bird has not become worn out.

materials.item: sheet of A4 paper or a page from a large notebook, for the paper bird
strips of newspaper, each 3 centimetres wide and 30 centimetres long
sticky tape, a ruler and scissors
the longest clear room or corridor in your home, at least 4 metres long
a start line, such as a dupatta laid on the floor or a strip of tape
something to measure with: a measuring tape, or floor tiles to count, or heel-to-toe steps
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: no tail, 30 centimetre tail and 60 centimetre tail. Write the five distances in each row. Then write the middle distance for each row.
experiments.context: In this experiment you throw one paper bird with no tail, with a short tail and with a long tail. You measure how far each one flies. Male long-tailed widowbirds fly with tails half a metre long.

setup.art: A folded paper dart on a table beside three newspaper strips, a ruler and a roll of sticky tape.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a paper bird. Cut three newspaper strips, each 30 centimetres long.

setup.art: A child standing behind a dupatta laid across a corridor floor, throwing a plain paper dart gently forward.
setup.caption: 2. Throw the paper bird five times with no tail. Measure each flight.

setup.art: The same paper dart with one newspaper strip taped to the back end, trailing behind in flight.
setup.caption: 3. Tape on a 30 centimetre tail. Throw five times and measure.

setup.art: The paper dart with a tail twice as long, made of two strips taped end to end, dipping towards the floor in flight.
setup.caption: 4. Make the tail 60 centimetres long. Throw five times and measure.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, in floor tiles

flow.do: Show your child the paper and the newspaper strips. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will throw a paper bird with no tail, with a short tail and with a long tail. Which will fly farthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which paper bird will fly farthest: no tail, short tail or long tail? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will fly farthest?
good: A tail keeps a kite steady, so it may help.
A tail adds weight.
The tail will drag in the air.

flow.parent: Many children expect the tail to help, because a kite flies better with a tail. Do not correct this. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Long Tail Test. You guess how a tail will change the flight of a paper bird.

flow.do: Fold the sheet in half the long way and open it. Fold the two top corners in to the middle line. Fold the two slanted edges in to the middle line. Fold the whole shape in half. Fold each wing down. Cut three newspaper strips. Throw three practice flights.
flow.say: Hold the paper bird under the middle, level with your shoulder. Push the paper bird forward gently, straight ahead. Try to throw the same way every time.
flow.kid: Fold the paper bird. Cut three strips of newspaper. Practise three gentle throws.
flow.parent: A gentle push is easier to repeat than a hard throw. If the paper bird hits the far wall, throw more softly or step further back.
flow.context: In this step of the Long Tail Test you fold the paper bird and practise a steady throw.

flow.do: Lay the start line. Your child throws the paper bird five times with no tail. Measure from the line to the place where the nose comes to rest. Record each distance.
flow.say: Stand behind the line. Throw five times with no tail. After each throw, we measure and write the distance.
flow.kid: Throw five times with no tail. Measure each flight. Write it down.
flow.context: In this step of the Long Tail Test you throw the paper bird five times with no tail.

flow.do: Tape one strip flat under the back end of the paper bird, so that 30 centimetres trail behind. Throw five times from the same line. Record each distance.
flow.say: Now the paper bird has a tail 30 centimetres long. Throw the same way as before. Watch how the bird moves in the air.
flow.kid: Tape on one strip as a tail. Throw five times. Measure each flight.
flow.context: In this step of the Long Tail Test you throw the paper bird five times with a 30 centimetre tail.

flow.do: Tape the other two strips end to end. Replace the short tail with this 60 centimetre tail. Throw five times and record. Then take the tail off and throw three more times with no tail.
flow.say: Now the tail is 60 centimetres long. Throw five times. Then we take the tail off and throw three more times, as a check.
flow.kid: Make the tail twice as long. Throw five times. Then throw three times with no tail.

check.q: In the Long Tail Test, why do you throw again with no tail at the end?
options: To check the paper bird still flies well
To give the thrower a rest
check.why: After many throws the nose may be bent and the folds may be loose. If the last no-tail throws match the first ones, the paper bird has not changed. Then the shorter flights were caused by the tail. If the last throws are much shorter, repeat the test with a fresh paper bird.

flow.context: In this step of the Long Tail Test you throw the paper bird with a 60 centimetre tail. Then you check the paper bird again with no tail.

flow.do: For each row, put the five distances in order and circle the middle one. Then ask your child for the three things below. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note.
flow.say: Find the middle distance for each tail. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Find the middle distance in each row. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What did the long tail do to the flight?
good: The paper bird slowed down sooner.
The tail fluttered and dragged.
The paper bird dropped earlier.

ask.q: A male widowbird's tail is half a metre long. What might the tail cost him?
good: He flies more slowly.
He uses more energy to fly.
A hunter may catch him more easily.

flow.parent: In most homes the paper bird with no tail flies farthest. The 60 centimetre tail cuts the flight to about half or less. Write down what you really found. The explanation: a paper bird has to push air aside while flying. A long strip has a large surface that rubs against the air and flutters. This rubbing is called drag, and it slows the paper bird down. A slower paper bird drops sooner. A real bird with a very long tail must work harder to fly. If the tail made little difference in your Long Tail Test, cut wider strips, about 5 centimetres, and try again.
flow.think: A long tail makes flying harder. So why do male widowbirds still grow one?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Long Tail Test. You compare the middle distances and say what the tail did.

activities.title: Pigeon Watch: ten minutes at the window

materials.item: a window, a balcony or a terrace from which you can see pigeons
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Watch pigeons for seven minutes. Count the bows, and count how often the other pigeon stays.

activities.record: Two tally rows. Row 1: each time a pigeon bows and turns in front of another pigeon. Row 2: each time the other pigeon stays near instead of leaving.
activities.context: In this activity you watch city pigeons for seven minutes. You count how often one pigeon bows to another, and how often the other pigeon stays.

setup.art: A notebook page with two rows labelled 'Bows' and 'The other pigeon stays', each with space for tally strokes.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two rows: 'Bows' and 'The other pigeon stays'.

setup.art: A child at a window looking at a ledge across the lane, where one pigeon with a puffed neck bows towards another.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for seven minutes. Put a stroke for every bow.

setup.art: The second pigeon flying off the ledge while the first one still stands with a puffed neck.
setup.caption: 3. Put a stroke in the second row only if the other pigeon stays near.

flow.do: Draw the two rows. Find a place from which you can see pigeons on a ledge, a roof or the ground. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: A male pigeon courts a female by puffing up his neck, bowing and turning in circles. Out of ten bows, how many times will she stay near him? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw two rows. Out of ten bows, how often will the other pigeon stay?
flow.parent: Pigeons court in every month of the year in Indian cities. Morning and late afternoon are the best times. If no pigeons come, try again tomorrow morning.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pigeon Watch. You get ready and guess how often a bowing pigeon is accepted.

flow.do: Watch for seven minutes. Your child puts a stroke for every bow. They add a stroke in the second row if the other pigeon stays near for a count of ten.
flow.say: Tell me each time one pigeon puffs up and bows to another. Then watch the other pigeon. Does she stay, walk away or fly off?
flow.kid: Watch for seven minutes. Count the bows. Count how often the other pigeon stays.
flow.parent: The pigeon who bows is nearly always a male. Male and female pigeons look alike, so the bowing is how you tell. Watch quietly from a distance.
flow.context: In this step of Pigeon Watch you count bows, and you count how often the other pigeon stays.

flow.do: Compare the two rows. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at your two rows. How many bows did you count? How many times did the other pigeon stay? Who was doing the choosing?
flow.kid: Compare your two rows. Who was doing the choosing?

ask.q: Most bows were refused. Why might a female pigeon refuse so often?
good: She may already have a partner.
She is comparing several males.
She is not ready to breed yet.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pigeon Watch. You compare the number of bows with the number of times the other pigeon stayed.

activities.title: Dance in Step: can two partners learn to move as one?

materials.item: a clear patch of floor, about three steps wide
a phone to film with, or a third person to watch
a handkerchief or a small towel, to toss

schedule.what: Dance six moves with a partner before practice and after practice, and count the moves that were out of step.

activities.record: Write the number of moves that were out of step in round 1 and in round 2.
activities.context: In this activity two people dance six moves together, as a pair of sarus cranes do. You count how many moves are out of step before practice and after practice.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up facing each other, one step apart, both bowing at the same moment.
setup.caption: 1. Face your partner. Learn the six moves in order.

setup.art: The two partners both leaping with arms spread like wings, slightly out of time with each other.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1: dance the six moves with no practice. Count the moves out of step.

setup.art: The same two partners after practice, both tossing a handkerchief up at exactly the same moment.
setup.caption: 3. Practise three times. Then dance round 2 and count again.

flow.do: Agree six moves in this order: bow, spread your arms, turn round once, lift one knee, leap, toss the handkerchief. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Sarus cranes bow, leap and spread their wings together. We will dance six moves with no talking. How many will we get in step the first time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Learn six moves: bow, arms, turn, knee, leap, toss. How many will be in step?
flow.context: This is the first step of Dance in Step. You learn six moves and guess how well you will keep in step.

flow.do: Round 1. Stand face to face. Start on a nod, with no counting aloud. Film it, or let a third person watch. Count the moves where one partner was late.
flow.say: No talking and no counting aloud. Watch me, and I will watch you. We start when I nod.
flow.kid: Dance the six moves. No talking. Watch your partner all the time.
flow.parent: With no watcher and no phone, each partner says after every move whether it felt together. Most pairs are out of step on three or four moves in round 1.
flow.context: In this step of Dance in Step you dance the six moves for the first time. You count the moves out of step.

flow.do: Practise the six moves together three times. Then dance round 2 and count the moves out of step again.
flow.say: Let us practise three times. Watch how I get ready for each move. Now we dance round 2 and count again.
flow.kid: Practise three times. Then dance again. Count the moves out of step.
flow.context: In this step of Dance in Step you practise with your partner and then count again.

flow.do: Compare the two counts. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the two counts. What did you watch on me, to know when to move?
flow.kid: Compare round 1 and round 2. What did you watch on your partner?

ask.q: Sarus crane pairs dance together for years. What might the dance do for them?
good: They learn each other's moves.
The dance keeps the pair close.
Partners who move together can work together at the nest.

flow.parent: A pair of cranes must take turns on the eggs and guard the chick together. Many scientists think that dancing together helps to keep the pair bond strong.
flow.context: This is the last step of Dance in Step. You compare your two rounds and say what helped you keep in step.

activities.title: The Blue Hunt: collect like a bowerbird

materials.item: a mat, a tray or a sheet of newspaper, to lay things on
a timer or a phone
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Collect small blue things for three minutes and small red things for three minutes. Count them and arrange a display.

activities.record: Write the number of blue things and the number of red things you found in three minutes each. Draw your display.
activities.context: In this activity you collect small things of one colour from around your home. A male satin bowerbird collects blue things for his bower in the same way. You find out which colour is harder to find.

setup.art: A child holding a blue bottle cap and a blue clothes peg, looking around a room for more small blue things.
setup.caption: 1. Collect small blue things for three minutes.

setup.art: Two heaps on a mat, one of small blue things and one of small red things, with a child counting them.
setup.caption: 2. Collect small red things for three minutes. Count both heaps.

setup.art: Small blue things laid out in a neat curved pattern on a mat, with a grown-up bending down to look.
setup.caption: 3. Arrange one colour as a display. Ask someone to inspect it.

flow.do: Explain the hunt. Each thing must be smaller than your child's palm and must not be precious or breakable. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: A male satin bowerbird collects blue things and lays them out for females to see. Which will be harder to find in our home: small blue things or small red things? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which is harder to find at home: small blue things or small red things? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blue Hunt. You guess which colour will be harder to collect.

flow.do: Set the timer for three minutes. Your child collects small blue things onto the mat. Set it again for small red things. Count both heaps and write the numbers.
flow.say: You have three minutes for blue. Go. Now three minutes for red. How many of each did you find?
flow.kid: Collect blue things for three minutes. Then red things. Count each heap.
flow.parent: Bottle caps, pegs, buttons, crayons, hair clips and toy bricks all count. Everything goes back to its place afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of the Blue Hunt you collect small blue things and small red things, and count them.

flow.do: Your child arranges the rarer colour as a display on the mat. A family member inspects it and says what they noticed first. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Arrange your rarer colour so that it looks its best. I will inspect it as a female bowerbird would. Then I will tell you what I noticed first.
flow.kid: Arrange your rarer colour as a display. Ask someone to inspect it.

ask.q: In a forest, blue things are rare. What does a big blue collection tell a female bowerbird?
good: He searched for a long time.
He is good at finding things.
He can guard his things from other males.

flow.parent: In a forest there are few blue things: some feathers, berries and flowers. Male bowerbirds also steal blue things from each other. Near towns they now collect blue bottle caps and straws, which are easy to find. In your home blue plastic may be common too. Whatever you found is the result.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Blue Hunt. You arrange a display of your rarer colour and have it inspected.

projects.title: Morning Song Count: three days at the window

materials.item: a window or a balcony
a clock or a phone timer
a notebook page with a table for three days

schedule.what: Count bird calls for five minutes soon after sunrise, and for five minutes at midday.
Count again at the same two times.
Count once more, then compare the three days.

projects.record: A table with three rows, one for each day. In each row write the number of calls in the morning count and in the midday count. Add a note about any singer you could see.
projects.context: In this three-day project you count bird calls for five minutes in the early morning and five minutes at midday. You find out when the birds near your home sing most.

setup.art: A child in pyjamas at an open window at sunrise, with a notebook, listening to birds on wires and rooftops.
setup.caption: 1. Soon after sunrise, count every bird call for five minutes.

setup.art: The same window at midday in bright sun, with the child counting again and one crow on a wall.
setup.caption: 2. At midday, count again for five minutes.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows and two columns of numbers, the morning numbers larger.
setup.caption: 3. After three days, compare the morning counts with the midday counts.

flow.do: Day 1. Within one hour after sunrise, count every bird call or burst of song for five minutes. Do the same at midday. Before the first count, ask for a guess.
flow.say: We will count bird calls at sunrise and at midday. At which time will we count more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count bird calls for five minutes at sunrise. Count again at midday.
flow.parent: One caw, one coo or one burst of song is one stroke. Do not worry about naming the birds. Crows, pigeons, mynas, koels, sparrows and magpie robins are common singers in cities.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Morning Song Count. You count bird calls soon after sunrise and again at midday.

flow.do: Day 2. Count at the same two times, from the same place. Try to see one singer and note where they sit.
flow.say: Same window, same times. Today, try to spot one singer. Where is that bird sitting? Why might they choose that place?
flow.kid: Count at the same two times. Find one singer. Where do they sit?
flow.wait: Do this the day after day 1
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Morning Song Count. You count again and look for one singer.

flow.do: Day 3. Count once more at both times. Then compare the three morning counts with the three midday counts. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at all six numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Count once more. Compare mornings with middays. Say what you found, and why.
flow.wait: Do this the day after day 2

ask.q: Why might birds sing most in the early morning?
good: The air is still, so sound carries far.
There is too little light to find food well.
A bird who sings at dawn shows that he came through the night in good shape.

flow.parent: In most places the morning count is clearly higher. Scientists call this the dawn chorus. They have several explanations, and they do not yet agree on one. In the breeding season the difference is largest.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Morning Song Count. You compare the morning counts with the midday counts.

challenges.title: Open and Shut: build a display that you can hide
challenges.problem: A fan-throated lizard must be noticed by a partner, and must not be noticed by a hawk. He keeps a bright throat fan folded away and flicks it out for a moment. Your problem is like his. Build a paper display that a watcher five steps away sees clearly when it is open. When it is shut, the watcher must not find it against a plain bedsheet.
constraints: Use only paper, colours and tape.
It must open in two seconds and shut in two seconds, with one hand.
When shut, it must lie flat against a plain bedsheet or a plain wall.
The watcher stands five big steps away.
The watcher gets a count of three to look each time.
materials: a plain bedsheet or a plain wall
general: Fold a paper fan that is bright on the inside and plain on the outside.
Make a flap that lifts to show a bright patch under it.
Colour one side of a card brightly, and turn it over to hide it.
creative: Make the outside match your bedsheet, so that the shut display is camouflaged.
Add a movement, such as a shake, so that the open display is noticed sooner.
Use a colour that stands out most against your own wall, and test two colours to find out.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Draw it first. Test it six times: three open and three shut, in a mixed-up order. Write how many times the watcher saw it when it was open, and how many times when it was shut.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a paper display that can be shown and hidden quickly. A fan-throated lizard and a peacock solve the same problem by folding their ornaments away.

setup.art: A child holding a closed paper fan flat against a pale bedsheet hung on a wall, hard to see.
setup.caption: 1. When shut, your display must be hard to find against the sheet.

setup.art: The same child with the fan flicked open, showing bright orange and blue inside.
setup.caption: 2. When open, it must be seen at once from five steps away.

setup.art: A grown-up five steps away with a hand over her eyes, about to look for a count of three.
setup.caption: 3. A watcher looks for a count of three. Test it open and shut.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Hang or spread the bedsheet. Ask what makes a thing easy to see and what makes it hard to see.
flow.say: Your display must be easy to see when open and hard to find when shut. What makes a thing easy to see? What makes it hard to see?
flow.kid: What makes a thing easy to see? What makes it hard to see?

ask.q: What makes a thing easy to see from far away?
good: A colour that differs from the background.
A big size.
Movement.

flow.context: This is the first step of Open and Shut. You think about what makes a display easy or hard to see.

flow.do: Your child draws a design and builds it. Check that it opens and shuts with one hand.
flow.say: Draw your idea first. Then build it. Show me that it opens in two seconds and shuts in two seconds.
flow.kid: Draw your idea. Build it. Open it and shut it with one hand.
flow.context: In this step of Open and Shut you design and build your paper display.

flow.do: Test it. The watcher stands five big steps away with eyes shut. Your child holds the display open or shut against the sheet. The watcher looks for a count of three and says 'seen' or 'not seen'. Do six turns.
flow.say: I will shut my eyes. Hold your display open or shut against the sheet. I will look for a count of three.
flow.kid: Hold your display open or shut. The watcher looks. Do six turns.
flow.context: In this step of Open and Shut a watcher tests your display six times, open and shut.

flow.do: Look at the six results. Change one thing and test twice more. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: When was your display seen, and when was it missed? Change one thing to make it better. What does a peacock do when he is not displaying?
flow.kid: What worked? Change one thing. Test it again.

ask.q: Why is a display that folds away useful to an animal?
good: A hunter cannot see it most of the time.
The animal shows the display only when a partner is near.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what failed as much as a display that worked.
flow.context: This is the last step of Open and Shut. You improve your display and test it again.

worksheets.title: Courtship: who displays and who chooses

items.p: What is courtship?
opts: Finding and winning a partner for having young
Building a home for the winter
items.why: Courtship is everything an animal does to find and win a partner for having young. It can be a display, a song, a dance, a nest or a gift.

items.p: Why does each species of cricket have a chirp pattern of their own?
opts: So partners of the same species meet
items.why: A female cricket walks towards the pattern of her own species. A pattern shared with another species would lead her to the wrong partner.

items.p: A show of colour, shape or movement that one animal gives for another to see is called a ____.
items.why: A display is made for the eyes. A peacock's raised train and a lizard's throat fan are displays.

items.p: The long feathers that a peacock raises are his tail feathers.
items.why: False. The long feathers are called the train, and they grow from his back. His real tail is short and brown, and it props the train up.

items.p: Match each animal to their courtship.
items.why: These are five kinds of courtship: a display, a song, a dance, a nest and a gift. Many animals use more than one kind.

items.p: Sort these courtship signals. Is each one for the eyes or for the ears?
items.why: Colours and movements are seen, so they need light and a clear view. Calls and songs are heard, so they also work at night and among leaves.

items.p: A peahen walks past three displaying peacocks and stays with one. Who chose?
items.why: The peacocks all displayed. The peahen compared them and stayed with one. In peafowl the female does most of the choosing.

items.p: In every species, only the male displays.
items.why: False. Both partners dance in sarus cranes and grebes. In the greater painted-snipe the female is the brighter one, and she courts the male.

items.p: Put these steps of a baya weaver's courtship in order.
items: The male weaves half a nest
He hangs under the nest and flaps his wings
A female goes inside and inspects the nest
a: The male weaves half a nest
He hangs under the nest and flaps his wings
A female goes inside and inspects the nest
items.why: The male builds first and displays at the half-built nest. The female inspects before she accepts. The nest is finished only after she has chosen it.

items.p: The part of the year when a species courts, mates and raises young is called the ____ season.
items.why: Most animals have a breeding season. It puts their young into the world when food is plentiful.

items.p: In the Long Tail Test, which paper bird usually flies the shortest distance?
opts: The one with the longest tail
The one with the short tail
items.why: A long strip drags against the air and slows the paper bird, so the bird drops sooner. If you chose 'no tail', look at your results table again.

items.p: Give two things that a chooser can learn from a courtship display.
items.a: One: the other animal is of her own species. Two: the other animal is healthy, or skilful, or good at finding food.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different things. Species, readiness to breed, health, skill and the ability to find food are all correct.

items.p: In the Eyespot Test, why must the three paper trains differ in only one way?
items.a: If the trains differed in two ways, I could not tell which difference changed the choices. With one difference, any change in the choices comes from the spots.
items.why: A strong answer says that a second difference would be a second possible reason for the result.

items.p: Draw a peacock displaying to a peahen. Label the train, one eyespot and the chooser.
items.a: A peacock with his train raised in a fan, facing a peahen. Labels: 'train' on the fan, 'eyespot' on one round mark, and 'chooser' on the peahen.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the peahen as the chooser. The train should rise from the back, not from the tail tip.
items.art: A blank box with a small outline of a peahen standing on the right.

items.p: Which of these animals stay together as a pair for many years?
items.why: A pair of sarus cranes may stay together for many years and raise chicks together. A peacock and a peahen part after mating, and she raises the chicks alone.

worksheets.title: Costs, seasons and many ways to pair

items.p: A male bullfrog is bright yellow for only a day or two. Why not all year?
opts: Bright skin is easy for hunters to see
The yellow washes off in rain
items.why: A bright colour is noticed by partners and by hunters. Showing the colour only at breeding time keeps the cost low.

items.p: Four species of frogs call in one pond. How does a female find her own species?
opts: By the pattern of the call
items.why: Each species has a call pattern of their own. She goes towards the pattern of her species, even if another call is louder or nearer.

items.p: A peacock sheds his train after the breeding season. What does he gain?
opts: Less to carry, and harder to see
items.why: The train is needed only for courtship. Without the train he has less to carry and is harder for a hunter to notice.

items.p: Why do many Indian frogs start courtship after the first heavy rain?
opts: Their tadpoles need pools of water
items.why: Frog eggs and tadpoles need water. Courtship that starts with the rain puts the tadpoles into full pools.

items.p: Female birds never sing.
items.why: False. A study in 2014 found that females sing in about seven out of ten songbird species with good records. In some species partners sing duets.

items.p: A satin bowerbird's bower is the nest where the eggs are laid.
items.why: False. The bower is a place for courtship only. After choosing a male, the female builds her own nest somewhere else.

items.p: Sort these animals by who looks after the young.
items.why: Animals raise young in many ways. In hornbills and cranes the pair shares the work. A peahen works alone. In jacanas and painted-snipes the father does the caring.

items.p: Three of these are made or brought for courtship. Which one grows on the body?
items.why: The fish, the nest and the collection are found or made. The train is an ornament, a part of the peacock's own body.

items.p: A peacock shakes his train 25 times each second. How many times does he shake it in 4 seconds?
items.why: 25 shakes each second for 4 seconds is 25 times 4, which is 100 shakes.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to test whether female birds prefer long tails.
items: Catch some males of one species
Make some tails longer and some shorter
Let the males go on their own patches
Count the new nests on each patch
a: Catch some males of one species
Make some tails longer and some shorter
Let the males go on their own patches
Count the new nests on each patch
items.why: The tails are changed first. The counting comes after the females have had time to choose. Malte Andersson tested widowbirds in this way in Kenya.

items.p: A frog who calls loudly is found by more females and by more bats. Why does he still call?
items.a: A frog who stays silent is safe from bats, but females cannot find him, so he has no young. A frog who calls takes a risk and may have young.
items.why: A strong answer weighs the gain against the cost. Being chosen matters as much as staying alive, because only chosen animals leave young.

items.p: Six choosers picked: 16 spots three times, 8 spots twice, 4 spots once. Is this strong evidence? Explain.
items.a: No, it is weak evidence. Luck alone would give about 2 picks to each train, and 3 is only one more. I would need many more choosers.
items.why: A strong answer compares the counts with what luck would give, and asks for more choosers.

items.p: Sarus cranes dance together even after years as a pair. Give one reason why this may help them.
items.a: Dancing together may keep the pair bond strong. The two birds must share the work of guarding the nest and feeding the chick.
items.why: A strong answer links the dance to working together as a pair. Any sensible reason is accepted.

items.p: A peahen stays with the peacock who has the fullest train. Scientists explain her choice in different ways.

views.says: A full train is hard to grow when a bird is ill. She is choosing a healthy father for her chicks.
She enjoys the look of the train. Her liking needs no other reason.
Her eyes already notice bright round shapes, such as berries. The eyespots catch the attention she already has.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say how a scientist could test your view.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that a costly display is hard for a sick animal to keep up. One test is to check whether the chicks of chosen males grow better.
items.why: Working scientists hold each of these views, and more than one may be true. A strong answer gives a reason and suggests a test.

items.p: Label three parts of this half-built baya weaver nest.
labels: The thin branch that the nest hangs from
The woven room where the eggs will lie
The opening where the female goes in
a: The thin branch: a snake struggles to climb along a thin branch
The woven room: it must hold the eggs and the chicks
The opening: the female goes in here to inspect the nest
items.why: A female weaver inspects the nest and the place where it hangs. Each part matters for the safety of her eggs.
items.art: A helmet-shaped half-built grass nest hanging from a thin branch over water, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A scientist changes the tails of some widowbirds and leaves others unchanged. Why leave some unchanged?
opts: To compare them with the changed birds
items.why: The unchanged birds show what happens with no change at all. Without them, nobody could tell whether the changed tails made a difference.

items.p: A scientist cuts a tail and glues the same piece back on. What does this check?
opts: Whether cutting and gluing alone changes the result
items.why: Catching, cutting and gluing might upset a bird. A bird with the same tail length after cutting shows whether the handling itself matters.

items.p: Suppose hunters became very common. What would probably happen to displays over many generations?
opts: They would become smaller or duller
items.why: With more hunters, the showiest animals are caught more often and leave fewer young. John Endler found duller male guppies in streams with more fish-eating fishes.

items.p: In jacanas the father raises the chicks. Which partner is larger and guards the patch of lake?
items.why: In jacanas the usual roles are swapped. The female is larger, guards the patch and may have several male partners. Each male cares for a set of eggs.

items.p: If most choosers pick the same paper train, they must all have the same reason.
items.why: False. A count shows what was chosen. It does not show why. One chooser may like many spots, and another may like a train that looks full.

items.p: A display that is hard to keep up when ill can tell a chooser about health.
items.why: True. If only a healthy animal can sing for hours or grow bright feathers, then the display carries news about health.

items.p: Match each courtship to what it may show a chooser.
pairs: A nest in a safe place
the singer has energy to spare
the caller is of her species
A big collection of rare things
the collector searches and guards well
items.why: Each kind of courtship gives a chooser a different kind of news. Scientists still argue about how much choosers use this news.

items.p: Twelve choosers each pick one of three paper trains. By luck alone, about how many picks would each train get?
items.why: 12 picks shared equally among 3 trains is 12 divided by 3, which is 4. A train with many more than 4 picks is worth noticing.

items.p: A place where many males display close together, and females come to choose, is called a ____.
items.why: Peacocks and blackbuck display on leks. A female can compare many males in one visit.

items.p: The Eyespot Test used human choosers. Why can its result not tell us what peahens prefer?
items.a: People and peahens are different species with different eyes and brains. To learn what peahens prefer, a scientist must change real trains and count what peahens do.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result about one kind of chooser cannot be passed to another kind. The method can be shared, but the result cannot.

items.p: In the Long Tail Test, the last no-tail throws were much shorter than the first ones. What should you do?
items.a: The paper bird has probably become bent or loose. I should fold a fresh paper bird and run the whole test again.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the paper bird changed during the test. Then the tail was not the only thing that changed.

items.p: On one island, many albatross pairs are two females who raise a chick together. What does this show?
items.a: It shows that animals pair in more than one way. Two birds who share the work can raise a chick, whoever they are.
items.why: A strong answer says that there is no single pattern of pairing in nature. Raising a chick depends on shared work.

items.p: A bird lives in thick, dark forest. Which would work better for courtship there: colour or song? Explain.
items.a: Song would work better. Leaves block the view and there is little light, so colours are hard to see. Sound travels round leaves and works in dim light.
items.why: A strong answer links the kind of courtship to the place. A child may also suggest a colour shown in a patch of sunlight, with a reason.

items.p: A pair of sarus cranes nests in a farmer's wet paddy field every year.

views.says: The cranes trample some of my young rice, and I lose a little of my crop.
This pair returns to the same field each year. If the nest is disturbed, they raise no chick that year.
Cranes have danced here longer than our village has stood. Let us guard the nest and share the farmer's loss.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about pairs and breeding seasons. Then answer one other view.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a pair has one breeding season each year, so a lost nest is a lost year. Another is that the farmer's loss is real and should be shared.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the fact that a pair breeds once a year, and takes the farmer's loss seriously.

items.p: Invent a courtship signal for an animal in muddy water. Draw the signal and name the sense used.
items.a: Any signal that does not need a clear view. A call, a drumming on the river bed, a smell, a touch or an electric pulse would all work. The drawing names the sense.
items.why: A strong drawing chooses a sense that works in muddy water. A colour display is not a good answer, because colours are hard to see in mud.
items.art: A blank box showing brown, cloudy water with the outline of one fish.

opts: Finding and winning a partner for having young
quiz.why: Courtship brings two animals of one species together and gives each a chance to choose. A song may also warn rivals, but its main work in courtship is to win a partner.

quiz.p: Each firefly species flashes in a rhythm of their own. What does the rhythm tell another firefly?
quiz.why: The rhythm is the code of the species. A firefly answers only the rhythm of their own species.

quiz.p: Which of these is a courtship dance?
opts: Two sarus cranes bowing and leaping
quiz.why: Sarus cranes bow, leap and spread their wings together. The dance helps to form the pair and to keep the pair bond strong.

quiz.p: A male kingfisher brings a fish to a female. What can the gift show her?
quiz.why: A partner who can catch fish now can probably catch fish for the chicks later. A gift is news about a skill.

quiz.p: In peafowl, who usually does the choosing?
quiz.why: Peacocks display, and each peahen compares several of them before she accepts one.

quiz.p: You want to know whether spots change what choosers pick. What must you do?
opts: Change only the number of spots
Change the spots and the paper colour
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing. If two things differ, you cannot tell which one changed the choices. One chooser is too few to show a pattern.

quiz.p: Why does a long newspaper tail shorten a paper bird's flight?
opts: The tail drags against the air
The tail makes the paper bird lighter
The tail pushes the paper bird forward
The tail hides the paper bird
quiz.why: A long strip has a large surface that rubs against the air and flutters. This drag slows the paper bird, and a slower paper bird drops sooner.

quiz.p: Which of these is a cost of a loud courtship call?
opts: A hunter can find the caller
quiz.why: A loud call reaches partners and hunters alike. Bats who eat frogs find calling frogs more easily. Being heard by partners is the gain, not the cost.

quiz.p: Which of these animals raise their young as a lasting pair?
quiz.why: A hornbill father feeds the mother and the chick for months, and the pair may stay together for years. A peahen raises her chicks alone.

quiz.p: A scientist wants to know whether female birds prefer long tails. What is the best test?
opts: Lengthen some tails, shorten others, count nests
Watch one bird for an hour
quiz.why: Changing the tails and counting what females do is a fair test. Watching one bird, or measuring one tail, cannot show a preference.

quiz.p: Which sentence about choosing is correct?
opts: In some species both partners choose
quiz.why: Females choose in many species, and in cranes and grebes both partners choose. Frogs, fishes, insects and mammals choose too. Humans are one choosing animal among many.

quiz.p: Many birds begin courtship when the days grow longer. Why does the timing matter?
opts: Chicks hatch when food is plentiful
quiz.why: Chicks need a great deal of food. Courtship at the right time of year puts the chicks into the world when insects, seeds or fruit are plentiful.

applications: People who protect rare animals let the animals choose their partners where they can. In a 2015 study, giant pandas paired with a partner they preferred had more cubs.
Bird counters listen for songs. Each species sings a pattern of their own. So a trained listener can count the species in a forest without seeing one bird.
Each species has a song pattern of their own. So phone apps can now name a bird from a recording of the song.
Bright lights at night hide the flashes of fireflies, and partners cannot find each other. Some forest camps switch off their lights in the firefly season.
Some farmers in Uttar Pradesh leave a sarus crane nest alone in their paddy field. This helps the same pair to raise a chick year after year.
A peacock feather makes blue and green with tiny stacked parts and only a brown colouring. Scientists copy this to make colours that never fade.

open_questions.q: What exactly does a peahen judge when she chooses a peacock?
open_questions.why_open: One team found that eyespot number matters, and another team found that it does not. She may judge the shaking, the call, the colours or all of them together.

open_questions.q: Do other animals find some things beautiful?
open_questions.why_open: Charles Darwin thought that birds have a taste for the beautiful. We can count what an animal chooses, but nobody has yet found a way to measure what the animal feels.

open_questions.q: Why do birds sing most at dawn?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several explanations: still air, poor light for feeding, and showing strength after the night. They do not yet agree on one.

open_questions.q: What does a female pufferfish judge in a sand circle?
open_questions.why_open: The circle was linked to the pufferfish only in 2011. Scientists do not yet know which part of the circle makes a female accept the male.

open_questions.q: Do animals who pair for years feel attached to each other, as people do?
open_questions.why_open: In prairie voles, who live in pairs, the pair bond needs the same body chemicals that help people to bond. What the voles feel cannot yet be measured.

maths.problem: In the Long Tail Test, five throws with no tail went 9, 7, 8, 3 and 8 floor tiles. What is the middle distance? Why is the middle a fairer number to use than the shortest throw?
maths.answer: The middle distance is 8 tiles. The throw of 3 tiles was a bad throw, and the middle value is not pulled down by it.
maths.explain: Put the distances in order: 3, 7, 8, 8, 9. The third of the five numbers is the middle one, which is 8. One bad throw does not change the middle.
maths.context: In the Long Tail Test you throw a paper bird five times and measure each flight. These are made-up distances.
maths.why_maths: Five throws give five different numbers. The middle one gives a fair single number for comparing the tails.

maths.problem: With no tail, the middle flight was 8 floor tiles. With the 60 centimetre tail, it was 4 tiles. What fraction of the flight was left? Each tile is 60 centimetres wide. How many metres shorter was the flight?
maths.answer: One half of the flight was left. The flight was 2 metres 40 centimetres shorter.
maths.explain: 4 out of 8 is one half. The flight was 4 tiles shorter, and 4 times 60 centimetres is 240 centimetres. That is 2 metres 40 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Long Tail Test you compare a paper bird's flights with no tail and with a long tail. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how much of the flight the tail took away. It works whatever the size of your room or your tiles.

maths.problem: In the Eyespot Test, 12 choosers each picked one of three trains. The 16-spot train got 7 picks, the 8-spot train got 3 and the 4-spot train got 2. If choosers picked by luck alone, about how many picks would each train get? Is 7 far from that?
maths.answer: About 4 picks each. 7 is nearly twice as many as 4, so the spots probably did change the choices.
maths.explain: 12 divided by 3 is 4. Luck would give counts near 4, such as 3, 4 and 5. A count of 7 beside counts of 3 and 2 is a big gap.
maths.context: In the Eyespot Test you ask people to choose one of three paper trains with 4, 8 or 16 spots. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what luck alone would give tells you whether your counts mean anything.

maths.problem: Hawk Overhead has 24 cards, and 6 are hawks. What is the chance that the first card is a hawk? You turn over three display cards. Now 21 cards are left, with 6 hawks. Has the risk of a hawk on the next card gone up or down?
maths.answer: The chance is 6 out of 24, which is one quarter. After three display cards the chance is 6 out of 21, so the risk has gone up.
maths.explain: 6 out of 24 is the same as 1 out of 4. With 21 cards left, the 6 hawks make up a bigger share of the pile. 6 out of 21 is more than 6 out of 24.
maths.context: Hawk Overhead is a card game. You turn over display cards for points, and a hawk card takes the points of that turn.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two fractions shows why each extra card in a turn is riskier than the one before.

maths.problem: In Pigeon Watch, a watcher counted 20 bows. The other pigeon stayed 2 times. What fraction of the bows were accepted? If the male bows 50 times in a morning, about how many times would the other pigeon stay?
maths.answer: One tenth of the bows were accepted. Out of 50 bows, about 5.
maths.explain: 2 out of 20 is the same as 1 out of 10. One tenth of 50 is 5. The real number will vary from morning to morning.
maths.context: In Pigeon Watch you count how often a pigeon bows, and how often the other pigeon stays near. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A fraction from a short watch lets you predict what a longer watch would show.

maths.problem: A male white-spotted pufferfish is 12 centimetres long. His sand circle is 200 centimetres wide. About how many times his own length is the circle? A child is 130 centimetres tall. How wide would a circle be that is the same number of times her height?
maths.answer: The circle is about 17 times his length. For the child, the circle would be about 22 metres wide.
maths.explain: 200 divided by 12 is 16 with 8 left over, so it is nearly 17. 130 times 17 is 2,210 centimetres, which is about 22 metres. That is as wide as two buses parked end to end.
maths.context: A male white-spotted pufferfish shapes a circle of ridges in the sand of the sea floor. A female inspects the circle.
maths.why_maths: Scaling the circle up to a child's size shows how much work the pufferfish puts into courtship.

This Class 4 unit covers courtship rituals and mate choice, and introduces the many ways of pairing by example. Competition between males, the theory of sexual selection, parental investment and the named family systems are left for sci.animals.courtship-and-mates.L5, as the curriculum says.

There is no lower-level unit of this subtopic. The prerequisite sci.animals.animal-babies.L2 and the units sci.animal-behaviour.animal-communication.L4, sci.animals.animals-around-us.L3 and sci.forces.flight.L4 were checked so that no experiment, game or story repeats. The peahen eyespot debate also appears in the communication unit as one challenging view. Here it is the centre of the Eyespot Test.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1871 Charles Darwin wrote that female animals choose their partners. He said that long tails and bright colours grew over many generations because females preferred them. Most scientists of his time did not accept this. Even his friend Alfred Russel Wallace doubted that a bird could have such a taste. They said that bright colours only helped animals to know their own species. For about a hundred years almost nobody tested the idea. Then, in 1982, Malte Andersson went to the grasslands of Kenya. Male long-tailed widowbirds there have tails about half a metre long. He cut the tails of some males short. He glued the cut pieces on to other males, which made their tails longer. He left some males as they were. Then he counted the new nests on each male's patch of grass. The males with the longest tails had the most new nests. In 1991 Marion Petrie showed that peahens also choose among peacocks. Darwin had been right that females choose.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in England, Malte Andersson of Sweden, working in Kenya, and Marion Petrie in England
how_we_found_out.when: Darwin's book The Descent of Man came out in 1871. Andersson published his widowbird test in 1982, and Petrie published her peafowl study in 1991.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That female animals have no preferences, and that bright colours only help animals to know their own species. Andersson changed the tails of widowbirds and showed that females nested most with the longest-tailed males.
how_we_found_out.art: A grassland in Kenya with a black male widowbird flying low, his very long tail trailing behind, and a scientist with a notebook counting nests in the grass.

roots.context: In this unit you counted what choosers pick, and you found that a long tail shortens a paper bird's flight. Here we ask what choosing has made, and whether beauty is in the thing or in the one who looks.

deep_truth.truth: In the Long Tail Test, the paper bird with the longest tail flew the shortest distance. A male long-tailed widowbird still grows a tail half a metre long. Female widowbirds choose long-tailed males, so those males have more young. So the choices of females have shaped the bodies of males, even where flying became harder.
deep_truth.habit: We think every part of a body is there to help its owner stay alive: legs to run, a beak to feed. A long tail does not help a widowbird stay alive. It is there because others of his kind preferred it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Long Tail Test the 60 centimetre tail cut the flight of the paper bird. In 1982 Malte Andersson lengthened the tails of some male widowbirds in Kenya. Those males had the most new nests on their patches of grass.

three.who_am_i: You have two parents, four grandparents and eight great-grandparents. Every one of your ancestors found a partner. If even one had not, you would not be here.
three.what_is_life: Most animals cannot make young alone. Their kind of life goes on only where two beings find each other and accept each other.
three.what_is_this_world: Much of the colour and song around you was shaped by choosers. A peacock's train and a magpie robin's song exist because, over many generations, partners watched and listened and chose.

roots.thread: Two animals begin as separate beings, and often as strangers. In courtship each one pays close attention to the other. Then one cell from each joins, and a new being begins from the two. Many wise teachers taught that many beings come from one source. This unit shows something that goes the other way. Two separate beings come together, and from the two a new life begins, again and again, in every generation.

teachings.teaching: The poet Valmiki sees a pair of krauncha birds together by a river. A hunter shoots the male, and the female cries out. Valmiki's grief comes out as a verse, which tradition calls the first shloka.
teachings.link: Many scholars think the krauncha is the sarus crane. The poem takes the bond between two birds seriously. Field studies agree that sarus pairs stay together for many years. Whether a crane grieves as a person does cannot yet be measured.

teachings.teaching: The poet asks: what is my mother to yours, and how did you and I ever meet? Yet, like red earth and pouring rain, our hearts have mixed.
teachings.link: The poem is about two people. It says plainly what happens in every pair: two beings who were strangers come to act together. Two sarus cranes calling in a duet show the same joining.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, The Descent of Man (1871), Part 2, the chapters on birds
teachings.teaching: Darwin wrote that birds have a taste for the beautiful. He said that female birds, by choosing over a long time, had added to the beauty of the males.
teachings.link: This is the idea that the Eyespot Test and the widowbird test are about. Darwin gave other animals a sense of beauty at a time when most scientists gave it only to humans.

science.text: Almost every animal with two parents begins when two cells join, one from each parent. So each of these animals carries instructions from two beings.
The scientist Richard Prum argues that birds feel pleasure in what they choose. He says this pleasure has shaped feathers and songs. Others say a display is only a report on health.

other_view.who: Alfred Russel Wallace, and many biologists today
other_view.view: A female bird need not judge beauty at all. Her eyes and brain may simply respond more strongly to a bigger or brighter signal. She then goes to the strongest one. On this view, words such as taste and beauty should be kept for humans until there is evidence for more.

playtest: This unit was read through step by step, as a family in a city flat would use the unit. Nobody has yet done the parts at home. The Eyespot Test (core) needs three sheets of the same paper and 28 dots. The dots can be sticker bindis or drawn with one pen. It needs at least six choosers. In a small family, send photos to relatives by phone, with the trains in a different order in each photo. There is no expected result: many families will find most picks for 16 spots, and some will not. The steps say to record what really happens and to compare the counts with what luck would give. The Long Tail Test (core) needs one sheet of paper, newspaper, tape and about 4 metres of clear floor. The expected result is that the 60 centimetre tail cuts the flight to about half or less. A paper bird thrown hard flies unevenly. So the steps ask for a gentle push, five throws and the middle distance. If the tail makes little difference, use strips 5 centimetres wide. Pigeon Watch (core) depends on pigeons. They court all year in Indian cities and are easiest to see in the morning and late afternoon. If none come, try again the next morning. Call and Answer needs a steel tumbler and a spoon, and its knock codes are made up for the game. Hawk Overhead plays well alone or with others, and a game to 20 points takes about ten minutes. Dance in Step needs a third person or a phone to judge the moves fairly. The Blue Hunt has no fixed result, because many homes have plenty of blue plastic. The Morning Song Count works best in the breeding season. In the city most of the calls will be crows, pigeons and mynas. No part needs a garden. Facts to treat with care: the number of eyespots on a train, about 150, varies from bird to bird. The shaking rate, about 25 times each second, is an average from one study. Three points are marked as debated. They are whether peahens choose by eyespots, whether a costly display proves health, and whether the train slows a peacock. Many scholars think the krauncha bird in the Ramayana is the sarus crane. This is not certain. The Kurunthokai poem and Darwin's words are given as paraphrases. The topic is kept plain for children of nine: the unit says that animals mate and that a new animal begins when two cells join. The unit goes no further. The three videos have no address yet.
